questions.q: Who is this course specifically written for, according to this lesson?
options: People whose daily work is SQL, dbt, and notebooks — not a generic software-engineering audience
Only professional software engineers with years of Git experience
People who have never used a computer before
Exclusively web application developers
questions.explain: This course grounds every example in real data work (SQL, dbt, notebooks) rather than a typical software-engineering repository.

questions.q: What are Git's three stages, in order?
options: Working directory, staging area, repository
Repository, staging area, working directory
Commit, push, pull
Branch, merge, rebase
questions.explain: A change moves from the working directory, into the staging area via git add, and into the repository via git commit.

questions.q: What surprises people coming from a 'just save the file' workflow, according to this lesson?
options: Git never assumes you want to save everything you've changed — you deliberately choose what goes into each commit via the staging area
Git automatically commits every change the instant a file is saved
Git deletes the working directory after every commit
There is no difference between saving a file and committing it
questions.explain: The staging step means you deliberately choose which changes belong in the next commit, rather than Git assuming everything you've touched should be saved together.

questions.q: Which of these is an example of a real problem this lesson says Git solves?
options: Two analysts editing the same dbt model on the same afternoon and silently overwriting each other's changes
A computer running out of disk space entirely
A SQL query executing too slowly
A dashboard's color scheme not matching brand guidelines
questions.explain: Concurrent, unmanaged edits to the same file — like two analysts editing the same dbt model — is exactly the kind of silent-overwrite problem version control is built to prevent.

questions.q: What does this course assume you already know coming in?
options: You're comfortable with SQL and ideally have touched a dbt project or notebook — but you don't need any prior Git experience
You've already used Git professionally for years
You have no computer experience of any kind
You are already a certified DevOps engineer
questions.explain: The course starts Git from zero in Lesson 2, but assumes SQL comfort and some dbt/notebook exposure, since later chapters build directly on that context.
